questions.question: 1. What is the correct precedence order for the operators used in this experiment?

explanations.a: Correct. Exponentiation has higher precedence than multiplication and division, which have higher precedence than addition and subtraction.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This places division above exponentiation, which does not match the precedence used for these operators.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This reverses the relative precedence of multiplication and division.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This places exponentiation below multiplication and division.

questions.question: 2. During infix-to-postfix conversion using a stack, where are pending operators temporarily stored?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Operators are not necessarily written to the output immediately when they are encountered.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Operands and pending operators have different roles during the conversion.
explanations.c: Correct. The operator stack temporarily stores operators until precedence and parentheses allow them to be moved to the output.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The input is processed as the source expression and is not the temporary operator storage.

questions.question: 3. When an operand is encountered while converting an infix expression to postfix, what is normally done with it?

answers.a: Push it onto the operator stack
answers.b: Append it directly to the postfix output
answers.c: Discard it until all operators are processed
answers.d: Replace it with the previous operator

explanations.a: Incorrect. The stack in this conversion procedure is used primarily for pending operators and parentheses.
explanations.b: Correct. An operand can be appended directly to the postfix output because its position does not depend on operator precedence.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Operands are essential parts of the resulting postfix expression and cannot be discarded.
explanations.d: Incorrect. An operand retains its identity and is not replaced by an operator.

questions.question: 4. When an operator is read, why may operators already on the stack be popped before the new operator is pushed?

answers.a: To preserve operator precedence and associativity in the postfix output
answers.b: To remove all operands from the expression
answers.c: To make the stack contain only operands

explanations.a: Correct. Popping applicable higher- or equal-precedence operators preserves the required evaluation order before the new operator is pushed.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Operand removal is not the purpose of popping operators during conversion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The operator stack is intended to hold pending operators and parentheses, not to be converted into an operand-only structure.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Popping operators does not reverse the input expression.

questions.question: 5. What is done when a left parenthesis $($ is encountered during stack-based conversion?

answers.a: It is appended immediately to the postfix output.
answers.c: It is placed on the operator stack.
answers.d: It causes every operand to be popped.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Parentheses are control symbols for grouping and are not included in the final postfix expression.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The left parenthesis must be remembered so that the corresponding grouping can be handled correctly.
explanations.c: Correct. A left parenthesis is pushed onto the stack to mark the beginning of a grouped subexpression.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Encountering a left parenthesis does not require all operands to be removed.

questions.question: 6. What is the role of a right parenthesis $)$ during infix-to-postfix conversion?

answers.a: Push it onto the stack and leave it there.
answers.b: Pop operators to the output until the matching left parenthesis is found, then discard the pair of parentheses.
answers.c: Append the right parenthesis directly to the postfix output.
answers.d: Convert the right parenthesis into an operand.

explanations.a: Incorrect. A right parenthesis signals the completion of a grouped expression and should not remain on the operator stack.
explanations.b: Correct. Operators inside the group are moved to the output until the matching left parenthesis is reached; the parentheses themselves are then discarded.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Parentheses do not appear in the final postfix expression.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A parenthesis is a grouping symbol, not an operand.

questions.question: 7. For the infix expression $a+b*c$, what postfix expression should a correct stack-based conversion produce?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This postfix sequence performs addition before the multiplication represented in the infix expression.
explanations.b: Correct. The higher-precedence multiplication becomes $bc*$ first, followed by addition with $a$, producing $abc*+$.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The plus operator is not positioned after both operands in this sequence.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The multiplication operator is not placed after both of its operands.

questions.question: 8. In a standard stack-based infix-to-postfix algorithm, what should happen to the remaining operators after the entire input expression has been scanned?

answers.b: They should be converted into operands.
answers.c: They should be popped from the stack and appended to the postfix output, subject to valid-expression conditions.
answers.d: They should be pushed back into the input expression.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Remaining operators may still be required to complete the postfix expression.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Operators retain their role as operators throughout the conversion.
explanations.c: Correct. After the input is exhausted, remaining pending operators are popped from the stack and appended to the output.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The input expression is not rebuilt by pushing operators back into it.

questions.question: 9. What is the time complexity of scanning an infix expression of $n$ tokens using a standard stack-based conversion algorithm, assuming each token is pushed and popped at most a constant number of times?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Processing all $n$ tokens requires work that grows with the input size.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The algorithm does not reduce the number of tokens to a logarithmic amount of work.
explanations.c: Correct. Each token is processed a constant number of times, so the overall time complexity is $O(n)$.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The standard stack-based conversion does not require a quadratic number of token operations.
